question: What is the best term for this patient’s horizontal eye movements? ( video missing )
explanation: This patient with a clear cause for cerebellar dysfunction shows exam findings typical of square wave jerks (SWJs). For those astute observers, the patient also had a right hypertropia (which can barely be appreciated in the video) related to a skew deviation following his cerebellar tumor excision. SWJs are a type of saccadic intrusion. Unlike nystagmus, square wave jerks lack a fast / slow phase and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees) although amplitudes can be greater than 5 degrees in which case the name “macrosquare wave jerks” may be used. Square-wave jerks are commonly seen as bilateral small horizontal shifts (or "intrusions") from fixation during examination followed by a pause (or "intersaccadic interval") and then a quick return to fixation. That intersaccadic interval is characteristically 200 msec when mapped with eye movement tracings. Interestingly the term square wave jerk arises from the square waveform on eye movement tracings (see reference links below for examples). SWJs can be physiologic but when there are more than 9 per minute it is typically pathologic. Common causes include cerebellar disease, Parkinson’s disease, and supranuclear palsy. An astute eye care provider will look for signs and inquire about symptoms of Parkinsonism in any patient exhibiting frequent SWJs. If there are additional concerns for Parkinsonism then referral to a Neurologist with experience in movement disorders is indicated. While it might be easy to mistake abundant SWJs for horizontal pendular nystagmus, the intersaccadic interval (time where eyes fixate without moving) is seen only in SWJs. There is clearly no fast phase / slow phase present in this case so jerk nystagmus is not a consideration. Ocular flutter is a sustained horizontal saccadic intrusion without intersaccadic intervals and has a broad differential diagnosis identical to that of opsoclonus. Volitional nystagmus, or voluntary nystagmus, is a skill that up to 8% of the general population can perform. While for some it is a fun party trick, it can lead to expensive, unnecessary work-ups in conversion disorder patients. The nystagmus is bilateral, conjugate and marked by high- frequency, low amplitude nystagmus that is usually (but not always) horizontal. Usually patients can’t sustain the nystagmus for more than a few seconds (although exceptions exist) and there are typically associated eyelid fluttering and convergence movements. One way to fish out voluntary nystagmus is to see if the nystagmus stops as you have the patient follow your finger on motility testing. References: 1. http://www.dizziness-and-balance.com/practice/nystagmus/SWJ.htm 2. http://www.neuroophthalmology.ca/textbook/e-figures/square-wave-jerks-waveforms What is the most accurate means to quantify the severity of an afferent pupillary defect (APD) in the clinic? A.The time required for release of the pupil upon swinging a light to the abnormal eye B.The speed and extent of reactivity of the pupil to light in the abnormal eye C.The visual acuity in the abnormal eye D.Neutral density filters High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Many clinicians do not quantify the severity of an APD in practice preferring instead to only document its presence. Some clinicians will comment on whether an APD is questionable, subtle, or brisk. Some clinicians will measure the severity of an APD by using neutral density filters. In a patient with a right APD, neutral density filters are held over the left eye starting with the least dense filter (usually 0.3 log units). The swinging flashlight test is then performed with the filter covering the left eye. If the right pupil still dilates immediately when the flashlight is swung from the left eye to the right eye then the APD is still present. The density of the filter over the left eye is increased to 0.6 log units and the swinging flashlight test is repeated. This continues until the APD has been "neutralized." If too strong of a filter is placed over the better eye then the APD will actually reverse. The density of the filter required to neutralize the APD defines the severity of the APD. The advantage of grading an APD is that it allows an additional objective means (along with visual acuity, color vision, and visual fields) to follow a patient for possible progression of optic nerve pathology. If only the presence of an APD is documented then it is impossible to know if the APD gets worse over time. Approximately what percentage of eyes affected by demyelinating optic neuritis demonstrate optic disc edema? A.35% B.55% C.75% D.95% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The optic neuritis treatment trial (ONTT) showed that most optic nerves (65%) in demyelinating optic neuritis were normal appearing. Also, the ONTT found that eyes with peripapillary optic nerve hemorrhages had a markedly reduced risk of developing multiple sclerosis compared to all eyes with optic neuritis. Which of the following types of nystagmus usually has a delayed onset presenting months to years following an inciting stroke of the brainstem? A.Oculopalatal myoclonus B.Periodic alternating nystagmus C.Upbeat nystagmus D.See-saw nystagmus High Yield: Yes Your Answer: C Correct Answer: A Explanation: Oculopalatal myoclonus (OPM) is very unique and is marked by bilateral acquired nystagmus that is vertical and pendular in nature. Associated with nystagmus there can be rhythmic movements of the face, soft palate, pharynx, tongue, larynx, diaphragm, or even the extremities. Patients may suffer recurrent involuntary noises from contraction of the larynx and/or diaphragm. It is usually caused by a brainstem stroke affecting the central tegmental tract which runs from the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla to the red nucleus in the midbrain. Cerebellar input from the flocculus connects to the inferior olivary nucleus and has some some poorly defined role in maintaining stability of the eye. The triangle formed by these three structures (the cerebellar flocculus, the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla, and the red nucleus in the midbrain) is called the triangle of Guillain-Mollaret (or alternatively the triangle of Mollaret). Disruption of fibers along this triangle of circuitry results in oculopalatal myoclonus. Interestingly, the onset of nystagmus usually occurs months to years after the inciting stroke. Also for unclear reason there is hypertrophy of the inferior olivary nucleus on MRI in these patients which is highly specific for oculopalatal myoclonus. Periodic alternating nystagmus (PAN) (answer choice B) is a peculiar form of nystagmus with a cyclical transition of right beating to left beating jerk nystagmus. For a short period in the middle of the cycle there may be no apparent or minimal nystagmus and there can even be shift null points depending on where in the cycle the patient is. A complete PAN cycle usually lasts around 4 minutes. PAN may be acquired from a lesion of the cerebellum (particularly the nodulus or uvulua) or may be congenital. Acquired PAN often improves with baclofen (high yield testing point). Upbeat nystagmus (UBN) (answer choice C) is characterized by a slow drift down followed by a corrective fast saccade up. UBN localizes to the brainstem (typically the medulla) and the anterior cerebellar vermis. Common causes include thiamine deficiency (which often starts as UBN and transitions to DBN with time), demyelination, stroke, and cerebellar degeneration. See-saw nystagmus (SSN)(answer choice D) is characterized by rhythmic alternating of one eye elevating and incyclotorting while the other eye simultaneously depresses and excylotorts followed by the reverse movement. SSN is highly localizable to the midbrain and parasellar region. It is not unusual for SSN patients to exhibit bitemporal hemianopic field defects and bilateral optic atrophy because the parasellar lesion causing the nystagmus also results in disruption of the nearby visual pathways. Hence SSN is a rare example of when both nystagmus and visual field defects can be caused by one lesion.

question: A 60-year-old Caucasian male comes in for a routine glasses check. His eye exam is essentially normal and he is getting ready to leave when he mentions that his chin has been numb for the last month. He denies any trauma and has no explanation for his symptoms. He has normal cranial nerve function except for subjective numbness in the chin region. What would be the most appropriate line of questioning considering his symptoms?

options.A: Ask about risk factors for and symptoms of diabetes
options.B: Ask about history of alcohol use
options.C: Take a detailed family history of neurological disease
options.D: Inquire about prior history of cancer

explanation: "Numb chin syndrome" or mental nerve neuropathy is highly concerning for malignancy. The most common associated malignancies affecting the mental nerve are lymphoma and metastatic breast carcinoma but many other malignancies have been reported to cause this syndrome including: osteosarcoma, fibrosarcoma, plasmacytoma, metastatic lung cancer, and metastatic prostate cancer. Sarcoidosis has also been described as a cause of mental nerve neuropathy.

question: Which of the following is NOT associated with palinopsia?

options.A: Medications including topiramate, clomiphene, and trazodone

explanation: Palinopsia is a phenomenon marked by the persistence or recurrence of images following removal of the stimulus from the visual field. The most common cause is a lesion of the parieto- occipital region (usually the non-dominant, right side of brain) with an associated contralateral hemi-field visual field defect. In this instance, the phenomenon usually occurs within the blind portion of the visual field. Also associated are topiramate, clomiphene, trazodone, and prior use of hallucinogenic drugs (especially LSD and mushrooms). Episodic migraine associated palinopsia has been described as well. There are isolated reports of palinopsia related to epileptiform activity in the parieto-occipital region although most neuro-ophthalmologists do not believe that palinopsia in most cases is a seizure-related phenomenon. Papilledema has not been associated with palinopsia. Vision can subjectively take on what color in digoxin toxicity? A.Yellow / Green B.Red / orange C.Blue D.Brown High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Chromatopsia is the illusion of vision exhibiting an abnormal color. Digoxin toxicity-related chromatopsia is usually described as a yellow (i.e. "xanthopsia") or yellowish green hue throughout the visual field. It is typically reversible with cessation or decreased dose of the drug. These visual effects can occur despite "normal" serum level of digoxin on lab testing. ERG may reveal cone dysfunction in these patients. Sildenafil (Viagra) has been reported to result in a blue chromatopsia and this illusion may be a harbinger of an underlying risk in certain individuals for more serious ocular pathology such as non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) due to sildenafil (and related erectile dysfunction (ED) drugs). The exact association between ED drugs and NAION is still quite controversial. Which of the following is true of focal occipital lobe seizures? A.They typically last for 1-2 seconds B.In children, they are usually associated with structural lesions such as tumors C.They typically manifest with unformed hallucinations or positive visual phenomena D.They usually occur without other motor signs of seizures The Patient with Illusions, Hallucinations, and Disorders of Higher Cortical Function High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: Occipital lobe seizures are usually a form of benign self-limited epilepsy in children (in other words not associated with a structural lesion of the brain) while in adults there is often a clearly identifiable structural lesion on imaging. Seizure activity of the primary visual cortex typically results in unformed positive visual phenomena such as binocular flashing lights and geometric shapes in the contralateral hemifield of the seizure focus. They usually last 1-2 minutes but can last hours and even days. They usually are associated with other signs such as rapid bilateral eyelid blinking, eye flutter, or eye deviation. Complex visual hallucinations are more typical of temporal lobe seizures or parietal lobe seizures (which are very rare). What is the name of the "nystagmus-like" eye movement that is not a true nystagmus but rather a type of saccadic intrusion? It lacks a fast / slow phase and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees). Usually witnessed when a patient is fixating, it results in horizontal shifting away from fixation followed by a brief pause and then returns back to fixation. A.Opsoclonus B.Square-wave jerk C.Superior oblique myokymia D.Ocular dysmetria Topic: The Patient with Illusions, Hallucinations, and Disorders of Higher Cortical Function High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Square-wave jerks (SWJs) are a "nystagmoid" eye movement that is not a true nystagmus but rather a type of saccadic intrusion. It lacks a fast / slow phase and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees). Square-wave jerks are commonly seen as bilateral small horizontal shifts (or "intrusions") from fixation during examination followed by a pause and then a quick return to fixation. They are often seen in normal patients but when there are more than 9 square-wave jerks per minute the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease or progressive supranuclear palsy should be considered (both commonly exhibit numerous square-wave jerks). Superior oblique myokymia is a high frequency monocular oscillation caused by spontaneous firing of the superior oblique muscle. Opsoclonus is also known as saccadomania and is a dramatic bilateral eye movement disorder marked by involuntary multidirectional saccades without an intersaccadic quiet interval. Ocular dysmetria is a over shoot or undershoot of the eyes upon refixation to a new target and is loosely suggestive of cerebellar pathology. which of the following is NOT a classic feature of Balint syndrome? A.Object agnosia B.Optic ataxia C.Ocular apraxia D.Simultagnosia High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Balint syndrome is due to bilateral parieto-occipital lesions. The classic triad includes optic ataxia, acquired ocular motor apraxia, and simultagnosia although most cases of Balint syndrome do not clearly demonstrate all three findings. The underlying etiology is usually either bilateral strokes or cortical dysfunction from a variant of Alzheimer's disease which predominately affects the parieto-occipital region known as posterior cortical atrophy (or the visual variant of Alzheimer's disease). Optic ataxia is essentially acquired poor hand-eye coordination caused by a disconnect between vision and motor functions. There are many other causes of poor hand-eye coordination so this is not that helpful in making a diagnosis of Balint syndrome. Ocular apraxia is difficulty initiating saccades. Simultagnosia is the most prevalent component of the Balint syndrome triad and is also arguably the most useful sign to look for on examination. It is the failure to understand the entire meaning of a picture despite retaining the ability to recognize isolated objects within the picture. In other words, patients with simultagnosia can not "see the forest through the trees." Simultagnosia is often tested for by using the "cookie theft picture" and asking the patient to give an account of what is happening in the picture. Object agnosia is the inability to visually recognize objects despite being able to recognize objects based on touch or description. Hallucinations and illusions are related but clearly distinct subjective visual phenomena with differing etiologies. Which of the following is associated with hallucinations as opposed to illusions? A.Metamorphopsia B.Pulfrich phenomenon C.Micropsia D.Photopsias High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Illusions are an optical or cortical distortion of an object seen in reality. Metamorphopsia describes an abnormal subjective curvature or waviness to objects that in reality are straight. It usually occurs as a result of macular disease such as macular degeneration or epiretinal membrane. The Pulfrich phenomenon is the illusion that an object moving perpendicular to a person's line of sight is actually moving toward them or away from them. Theoretically, it could be seen in any disease affecting the conduction of visual information in one optic nerve more than the other. It is usually described in patients who have partially recovered following a bout of optic neuritis. Micropsia is the illusion that objects appear smaller than they should and is indicative of macular pathology, parietal lobe pathology, or an unusual migraine headache related phenomenon known as the "Alice in Wonderland" effect. Photopsias associated with cancer associated retinopathy, MEWDS, AZOOR, birdshot chorioretinopathy, and PVD are all simple, unformed hallucinations because they do not arise from distortion of an object in reality. A 78-year-old man presents six months following a stroke. He is left with a right-sided visual field defect but retains 20/20 vision in both eyes. The patient’s greatest complaint is difficulty with reading. When given a sample text to read, the patient cannot form any of the words, and instead reads each letter individually. The patient otherwise speaks and writes fluidly, and easily comprehends the examiners commands. The patient’s lesion localizes best to which of the following? A.Left occipital lobe B.Left parietal lobe C.Left occipitotemporal lobe D.Right optic nerve High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The patient has alexia (inability to read) without agraphia (inability to write) which localizes to a lesion of the left occipital lobe, with ipsilateral involvement of the splenium of the corpus callosum and adjacent periventricular white matter. The disrupted pathway that is responsible for the deficit is shown in the image. The left angular gyrus converts written to spoken language and receives visual input from the occipital lobe. If a lesion of the left occipital lobe occurs, visual information can only be received from the right occipital lobe via outflow from the corpus callosum and periventricular white matter. Simultaneous involvement of the outflow tract and left occipital lobe will therefore leave patients with alexia and a right homonymous hemianopsia. However, patients will be able to write, speak, repeat, and comprehend without difficulty. The cause of the lesion is most commonly a posterior cerebral artery distribution stroke. The video shows an example of a patient with a new hemorrhagic stroke involving the left occipital-parietal lobe and splenium of the corpus callosum. He is able to write words that are prompted to him but is immediately unable to read back. Less commonly, patients can present with alexia without agraphia with a preserved visual field. This may be possible if the lesion spares the striate cortex of the left occipital lobe, but still interferes with the transfer of information from the left and right occipital lobes to the left angular gyrus. WRONG ANSWERS: • B. The parietal lobe is involved in the “where” pathway of higher cortical visual function that involves spatial recognition of objects. Right parietal lesions can result in left sided hemineglect and difficulty with localization of objects in the left visual field. Less commonly, left parietal lesions can result in right sided neglect, but this tends to be less severe and recovers more quickly. • C. The occipitotemporal lobe is involved in the “what” pathway of higher cortical visual function that involves object recognition. Lesions of this pathway can lead to visual agnosia (difficulty with object recognition), hemiachromatopsia (loss of color perception in one hemifield), and prosopagnosia (difficulty with facial recognition). • D. A right optic nerve lesion would not be expected to produce a hemifield defect. Numerous (> 9 per minute) square-wave jerks can be a sign of what disease? A.Parkinson's disease B.Occipital lobe stroke C.Lead poisoning D.Alzheimer's disease High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Square-wave jerks (SWJs) are a "nystagmoid" eye movement that is not a true nystagmus but rather a type of saccadic intrusion. It lacks a fast / slow phase and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees). Square-wave jerks are commonly seen as bilateral small horizontal shifts (or "intrusions") from fixation during examination followed by a pause and then a quick return to fixation. SWJs are often seen in normal patients but when there are more than 9 per minute, the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease or progressive supranuclear palsy should be considered (both commonly exhibit numerous square-wave jerks).

question: Which of the following is true of focal occipital lobe seizures?

options.B: In children, they are usually associated with structural lesions such as tumors
options.C: They typically manifest with unformed hallucinations or positive visual phenomena

explanation: Occipital lobe seizures are usually a form of benign self-limited epilepsy in children (in other words not associated with a structural lesion of the brain) while in adults there is often a clearly identifiable structural lesion on imaging. Simultaneous involvement of the outflow tract and left occipital lobe will therefore leave patients with alexia and a right homonymous hemianopsia. However, patients will be able to write, speak, repeat, and comprehend without difficulty. The cause of the lesion is most commonly a posterior cerebral artery distribution stroke. The video shows an example of a patient with a new hemorrhagic stroke involving the left occipital-parietal lobe and splenium of the corpus callosum. He is able to write words that are prompted to him but is immediately unable to read back. Less commonly, patients can present with alexia without agraphia with a preserved visual field. This may be possible if the lesion spares the striate cortex of the left occipital lobe, but still interferes with the transfer of information from the left and right occipital lobes to the left angular gyrus. WRONG ANSWERS: • B. The parietal lobe is involved in the “where” pathway of higher cortical visual function that involves spatial recognition of objects. Right parietal lesions can result in left sided hemineglect and difficulty with localization of objects in the left visual field. Less commonly, left parietal lesions can result in right sided neglect, but this tends to be less severe and recovers more quickly. • C. The occipitotemporal lobe is involved in the “what” pathway of higher cortical visual function that involves object recognition. Lesions of this pathway can lead to visual agnosia (difficulty with object recognition), hemiachromatopsia (loss of color perception in one hemifield), and prosopagnosia (difficulty with facial recognition). • D. A right optic nerve lesion would not be expected to produce a hemifield defect. Numerous (> 9 per minute) square-wave jerks can be a sign of what disease? A.Parkinson's disease B.Occipital lobe stroke C.Lead poisoning D.Alzheimer's disease High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Square-wave jerks (SWJs) are a "nystagmoid" eye movement that is not a true nystagmus but rather a type of saccadic intrusion. It lacks a fast / slow phase and characteristically has a small amplitude (0.5 degrees to 5 degrees). Square-wave jerks are commonly seen as bilateral small horizontal shifts (or "intrusions") from fixation during examination followed by a pause and then a quick return to fixation. question: What is the next most appropriate step?
explanation: This child has septo-optic dysplasia (SOD) which is a congenital disease characterized by midline brain development abnormalities and unilateral or bilateral optic nerve hypoplasia. Vision can range from near normal to severely impaired. Nystagmus is frequently present and develops around age 1-4 months when the pathways required for normal fixation typically mature. All children with optic nerve hypoplasia should have an MRI of the brain and an endocrine evaluation because anomalies in brain development and hypopituitarism are common. Growth hormone (GH) deficiency is the most common endocrinopathy found in approximately 70% of children with SOD while hypothyroidism, adrenocorticotropic hormone deficiency, and diabetes insipidus are less common. Any disease with a highly effective treatment (hormone replacement in this instance), is high yield on standardized tests so commit these facts to memory. An ERG would not be helpful in this case because the patient's optic nerves are hypoplastic and can explain the patient's poor vision and nystagmus. There is no need to look for a retina etiology. There are only isolated reports of familial SOD so genetic counseling is not necessary. An FA would have no utility in this situation. The coronal section of a T1-weighted MRI above demonstrates the absence of a septum pellucidum. As you may recall from medical school neuro-anatomy, the septum pellucidum is a thin, vertical membrane separating the left and right lateral ventricles of the brain. The structure itself has no known function and it is not rare to find normal individuals with an absent septum pellucidum on MRI. In some individuals, however, agenesis of the septum pellucidum is a sign of septo-optic dysplasia (aka "de Morsier syndrome") supported in this patient by his hypoplastic optic nerves. Responding to a request from our users, below you can see a modified version of this patient's optic nerves to better highlight the pathology. The inner green circle indicates the margin of this patient's actual hypoplastic optic nerve consisting of retinal ganglion cell axons, the area from the inner green circle to the outer black circle is a region of retinal atrophy in the location of the intended scleral canal (in other words where the optic nerve was supposed to have inserted if it were of normal size). This finding is sometimes referred to as the "double ring" sign. The optic nerve hypoplasia in this case is more obvious in the left eye (center image). It is not unusual for there to be asymmetry in the degree of optic nerve hypoplasia in any one given patient- some patients with SOD may even have one completely normal appearing optic nerve. Which of the following is least likely to occur with a diagnosis of optic disc drusen (ODD)? A.slowly-progressive nasal visual field defects respecting the horizontal meridian B.permanent decreased central visual acuity C.peripapillary choroidal neovascular membrane (CNVM) formation D.transient visual obscurations (TVOs) Neuro-ophthalmology High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Optic disc drusen are proteinaceous nodules that can be calcified. They usually remain buried deep in the optic nerve early in life and then extrude themselves over time. As they surface at the entrance of the nerve fiber layer to the optic disc, they are theorized to block axoplasmic flow. This cessation of axonal function may lead to the "nerve fiber layer type" progressive visual field defects exhibited in ODD. Because they disrupt normal architecture of the retina and nerve head, they can be associated with CNVM formation. A small percentage of patients (< 10%) may suffer transient visual obscurations lasting seconds believed to be due to transient ischemia of the nerve head (episodes similar to TVOs from papilledema). Decreased central visual acuity is a harbinger of other pathology unrelated to ODD and should prompt a work-up for compressive lesions. Rarely, ODD is associated with non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy.

question: A 75-year-old veteran with a 60 pack-year history of smoking and alcohol abuse comes in with a complaint of 2 years of progressive vision loss. Which optic nerve appearance (A-D) would you expect in this patient taking into account the visual field shown above? (note that the right eye shows similar fields and nerve appearance)
explanation: The visual field presented is a Goldmann visual field demonstrating a central scotoma. Of the pictures shown, image D showing mild to moderate temporal pallor would correspond best to this visual field defect and history. Temporal pallor is a very non-specific sign of damage to the optic nerve and is associated with many different types of visual field defects from damage to the optic nerve. Image A shows a normal optic nerve head with a small cup-to-disc ratio (“disc at risk”). A disc at risk without swelling is not associated with any visual field defect. Image B shows severe disc edema related to elevated intracranial pressure. Papilledema is associated with enlargement of the blind spot in the early stages and nerve fiber layer defects in the later stages. Central vision is typically spared until the late stages in papilledema similar to glaucoma. Image C shows a glaucomatous optic nerve with prominent cupping and a focal notch at about 5 o’clock. Glaucoma is classically associated with nerve fiber layer type defects such as nasal steps, arcuate defects, and altitudinal defects. It would be highly atypical for an optic nerve with prominent glaucomatous cupping and notching of the neuro-retinal rim to demonstrate an isolated central visual field defect. Image D shows mild to moderate temporal pallor which can be associated with many different visual field defects including isolated central visual field defects.

question: in the axial cut of the FLAIR sequence MRI shown above, what structure does the tip of arrow "A" touch?
explanation: The superior ophthalmic vein begins superonasally in the orbit at the junction of the supratrochlear, supraorbital, and angular veins. It then passes posterolaterally in the superior portion of the orbit (superior to the optic nerve and inferior to the superior rectus muscle) before exiting the orbit at the superior orbital fissure and draining into the cavernous sinus. The importance of this structure should not be underestimated since enlargement of the SOV is an indicator of poor venous drainage through the cavernous sinus. SOV enlargement is a prominent feature in anteriorly draining carotid cavernous fistulas and in cavernous sinus thrombosis. Cranial nerves can be seen on MRI but would not be nearly as prominent as the SOV seen here (this SOV is not pathologically enlarged). Arrow "B" points to the left optic nerve. Arrow "C' points to the left optic tract. Arrow "D' points to the midbrain (identifiable by the “mickey mouse” sign).

question: What is the diagnosis in this case?
explanation: This is a classic presentation and video of ocular neuromyotonia of the right abducens nerve. Ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) is a rare diagnosis which can cause episodic diplopia. Most commonly associated with previous skull-base radiation treatment, the onset of this disease is usually months-to-years after the radiation treatment. The diplopia episodes last from seconds to minutes and are generally very stereotypical involving the same cranial nerve innervating the same muscles every episode. ONM can affect any muscle innervated by any ocular motor cranial nerve (CN III, IV, or VI) and the diplopia is often triggered by activation of the involved nerve or muscle as in this case. In other words, this patient with right abducens involved ONM triggers his episodes by looking to the right and increasing innervational tone to the right lateral rectus muscle. Similar to this patient, looking away from the involved muscle (thus decreasing innervational tone to the involved muscle / nerve) often helps to break an attack. This patient’s video shows a fascinating additional finding of palpebral fissure narrowing on the right side with apparent globe retraction when he attempts to look left during an attack of ONM. This occurs because ONM defies Sherrington’s law of reciprocal innervation. According to this law, when the right medial rectus contracts the right lateral rectus should relax. In this case during the attack there is simultaneous contraction of both the lateral rectus and the medial rectus leading to impaired adduction in the right eye and temporary right globe retraction into the orbit with apparent ptosis. Once the ONM episode resolves the patient’s enophthalmos and ptosis resolve. ONM is thought to occur because of ephaptic neural transmission which occurs when there is conduction of neural impulses across parallel neurons. In normal neuronal impulses, conduction between neurons occurs exclusively at synapses. When damage has occurred to the myelin of cranial nerves 3,4,or 6 then abnormal “cross-talk” between parallel neuron axons can occur leading to a pathologic increase in innervational tone in that nerve or nerve branch. The other simple way to think of it is a “short circuit” causing a transient increase in tone. ONM typically responds very well to anticonvulsant treatment (e.g. carbamazepine or gabapentin). Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an excellent consideration in any patient with intermittent diplopia. MG is a variable disease and would virtually never be expected to cause the exact same type of diplopia for 5 years. Furthermore, between episodes this patient’s alignment was completely normal. In MG, diplopia episodes typically last much longer, are more variable in quality, and are accompanied by evidence of fatigability on exam. This patient had no fatigue on prolonged upgaze and no orbicularis oculi weakness which are two of the most helpful tests on exam for patients with ocular involvement by MG. Seizures essentially never cause isolated unilateral eye movement abnormalities. Furthermore, a seizure causing recurrent bilateral eye movement abnormalities in isolation would still be extremely unlikely. Duane syndrome (DS) is a congenital eye movement disorder thought to be due to agenesis or dysgenesis of the 6th nerve nucleus and cranial nerve resulting in failure to abduct and/or adduct (depending on the subtype of Duane syndrome). DS comes in 3 forms depending on whether there is abnormal abduction (type 1), adduction (type 2), or both (type 3). While type 2 DS could cause impaired adduction with globe retraction on attempted adduction, it would result in constant rather than intermittent motility deficits and is congenital (not acquired as in this case).

A 20-year-old female presents with progressive oscillopsia and blurred vision in both eyes over the past 1 year. The video above demonstrates abnormal eye movements. ( there is video missing ) What additional exam finding would be most likely in this patient? A.Bilateral optic atrophy B.Open angle glaucoma C.Keratoconus D.Cone dystrophy Neuro-ophthalmology High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: This patient exhibits see-saw nystagmus (SSN) which is a relatively rare but highly testable form of nystagmus for several reasons. First SSN is very unique in its waveform. Second, SSN is highly localizable to the midbrain and parasellar region. Most other forms of nystagmus are either not highly localizable or localize to the more caudal portion of the brainstem (pons, medulla, or the cervicomedullary junction). SSN is often caused by sellar and parasellar mass lesions (e.g. pituitary adenomas, craniopharyngiomas) and thus it is not unusual for SSN patients to exhibit bitemporal hemianopic field defects and bilateral optic atrophy. The same pattern of visual field defects and SSN can be seen in traumatic chiasmopathy following head trauma. SSN is a rare example of when both nystagmus and visual field defects can be caused by one lesion. While there are surely a few patients with glaucoma, keratoconus, or cone dystrophy AND SSN by chance, these other diseases are not highly associated with SSN. SSN characteristically results in rhythmic alternating of one eye elevating and incyclotorting while the other eye simultaneously depresses and excylotorts followed by the reverse movement. Typically there is a pendular rhythm to the nystagmus but it may also exhibit a “hemi see-saw” or jerk pattern in which the eyes have a slow phase of torsion followed by a fast corrective phase. This patient has a jerk see-saw pattern with the slow phase torsional movement towards the left shoulder followed by a quick jerk towards the right shoulder. The name see-saw is an excellent mnemonic actually. Imagine 2 large eye balls on a see- saw that is constantly pivoting (see diagram below and imagine the fulcrum is the patient’s nose). The eyeball on the high-side is going to roll down (incyclotort) while the low-side eyeball is also going to roll down (excyclotort). When the see saw pivots the other way each eye will cyclotort the other way. SSN is not always acquired and may be congenital in which case it might be isolated idiopathic or associated with major structural brain abnormalities such as achiasma (absence of chiasm) or rarely septo-optic dysplasia. Interested in learning more about SSN, check out this excellent eyerounds case from University of Iowa: http://www.eyerounds.org/cases/case23.htm A 22-year old otherwise healthy male sequentially loses vision in both eyes (one eye then the other) to the level of hand motions over two weeks. There is no associated eye pain. The exam is unremarkable except for fine peri-papillary telangiectasias and a subtle elevation of both optic nerve heads. A fluorescein angiogram (FA) is performed and shows no leakage from the optic discs.

What is the ideal length of a temporal artery biopsy to optimize diagnostic yield? A.1 mm B.3-6 mm C.10 mm D.20-30 mm Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The "ideal" length of a temporal artery biopsy to optimize diagnostic yield is 20-30 mm (or 2-3 cm). A negative temporal artery biopsy does not rule out GCA (giant cell arteritis). The rate of false negative temporal artery biopsies is estimated to be 3-9%. This relatively high rate is thought to be related to the discontinuous vasculitic involvement of the temporal artery in GCA termed "skip lesions". A contralateral temporal artery biopsy can be attempted in highly suspicious cases. As an aside, the current BCSC states that "... biopsy segments should be 2–3 cm long" while the BCSC Neuro book recommends a 3-6 cm biopsy length. In clinical practice, the longer the segment the better to avoid a false negative result. explanation: "Pseudotumor cerebri" is also known as idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). Technically speaking, IIH can only be diagnosed if increased intracranial pressure (ICP) is measured (via lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position) in the absence of other causes of increased ICP (e.g. CNS mass, dural venous thrombosis, systemic vasculitis, etc). In addition, a normal CSF composition should be documented to rule out a meningeal cause of increased ICP. CSF pleocytosis refers to an increased cell count in CSF fluid (usually increased white blood cell count). Increased white cells in the CSF could indicate an infectious, malignant, or inflammatory CNS process. Note: the opening pressure typically needs to be greater than 25 cmH2O to be considered "elevated." explanation: The main point of this question is whether or not a patient with optic atrophy needs a workup if it appears to be due to non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). The key to this question is whether or not the patient fits the clinical picture for NAION and had documented optic nerve swelling at the time of vision loss. This patient, for instance, is a set-up for NAION (numerous vasculopathic risk factors and a small cup-to-disc ratio in the unaffected eye). Because we don't know when the event occurred, however, and whether he had optic disc swelling with the event, there is no way to know that he does not have a compressive optic neuropathy or some other type of optic neuropathy (syphilitic or arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy). At the very least this patient requires an MRI of the orbits and syphilis studies (RPR / FTA-ABS). Additional testing to consider for optic atrophy of unknown etiology (with low yield in this particular case) include ESR, B-12/folate, ACE, CXR, and ANA in search of possible lupus, sarcoidosis, and nutritional neuropathy. A 35-year old female gives birth to a healthy child but one day post-partum develops sudden binocular diplopia and severe headaches. Visual acuity is 20/20 OU but your exam reveals a right pupil involving third nerve palsy, a left sixth nerve palsy, and a symmetric bitemporal hemianopia. A head computed tomography (CT) was performed and showed “no acute intracranial process.” What would be the most helpful measure to confirm the diagnosis? A.Computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the brain B.MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of the brain C.Electromyography (EMG) D.MRA (magnetic resonance angiography) of the brain High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: This is a classic presentation for pituitary apoplexy, or hemorrhage into the pituitary with sudden pituitary expansion. Most cases of pituitary apoplexy occur due to hemorrhage into a pituitary adenoma. MRI of the brain is the imaging study of choice for optimal visualization of the chiasm to make this diagnosis. CTA or MRA would be the study of choice to look for an aneurysm which in theory could cause a right pupil involving 3rd nerve palsy and a left 6th nerve palsy due to increased intracranial pressure but would be unlikely to cause a symmetric bitemporal hemianopia (typically causes asymmetric visual field deficits because it is not a midline structure). EMG is one study used to evaluate for myasthenia gravis (MG) and is always good to consider in any extraocular motility deficit (especially bilateral deficits). MG does not cause headache and would not result in a bitemporal hemianopia. A CT of the head is quick, easy to obtain, and can diagnosis pituitary apoplexy but is not sufficiently sensitive to rule out the diagnosis. By far the best imaging study for evaluation of the sellar / parasellar region of the pituitary, cavernous sinus, and optic chiasm is an MRI. Often demyelinating optic neuritis must be distinguished from non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). Which of the following features is most characteristic of demyelinating optic neuritis and most helpful to distinguish the two entities at the time of initial presentation? A.Optic disc edema in the involved eye B.Altitudinal visual field loss C.Eye pain D.Poor visual acuity Hight yield Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: Eye pain (usually worse with eye movement) is present in 92% of patients with optic neuritis according to the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT). Eye pain is very unusual in NAION and when it occurs rarely it is described as a mild ache (which is not worse with eye movements). The ONTT also showed that most eyes with optic neuritis (65%) have normal appearing optic nerves but 35% do have swollen nerves. NAION always presents with a swollen optic nerve at the time of acute vision loss. Altitudinal visual field loss is characteristically seen in NAION but is also seen in 15% of patients with optic neuritis so it is not a reliable distinguishing characteristic. Eyes with optic neuritis recover to a level of 20/40 or better in 91% of cases so the visual prognosis is excellent. In contrast approximately 40% of eyes with NAION have vision worse than 20/200. Vision recovery in NAION (note that answer choice D is poor visual acuity at presentation rather than after recovery) occurs in about 40% but is usually not nearly as dramatic as in optic neuritis. One excellent distinguishing feature (not listed as an option here) is optic nerve enhancement on orbital MRI. In those challenging cases where clinical distinction is not possible based upon patient demographics, exam, and history then MRI with orbital sequences may be very helpful. The sensitivity of a good quality orbital MRI to show optic nerve enhancement in optic neuritis is over 90%. The optic nerve never shows enhancement in NAION. Which of the following is false regarding optic nerve pits? A.they can be gray, white, or yellow in color B.they are associated with serous macular detachments in 25-75% of cases C.they generally occur in eyes with poor visual acuity (e.g. visual acuity < 20/200) D.they can be associated with nerve fiber bundle visual field defects (e.g. arcuate scotoma) High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: C Explanation: The visual acuity in eyes with optic nerve pits is typically normal except in the setting of serous macular detachment (which is a relatively common event in eyes with optic nerve pits). A patient with a recent episode of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) has a right afferent pupillary defect (APD) on examination. Which of the following would be expected to be seen on examination? A.anisocoria with the right pupil being larger than the left pupil in dim light B.anisocoria with the left pupil being larger than the right pupil in dim light C.a relatively diminished consensual pupillary constriction in the left eye when shining a light in the right eye D.a relatively diminished consensual pupillary constriction in the right eye when shining a light in the left eye High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: The presence or absence of an APD has no bearing on the symmetry of pupil size. In other words, an APD does not cause anisocoria. In this case, an APD in the right eye is due to diminished function of the afferent input of the right optic nerve and has no bearing on the efferent system of the right eye. Therefore the right eye should constrict normally in response to a light stimulus to the left eye (normal consensual response). The left eye, however, will not constrict normally to a light stimulus in the right eye because of the diminished afferent function of the right eye.

question: A 35-year old female gives birth to a healthy child but one day post-partum develops sudden binocular diplopia and severe headaches. Visual acuity is 20/20 OU but your exam reveals a right pupil involving third nerve palsy, a left sixth nerve palsy, and a symmetric bitemporal hemianopia. A head computed tomography (CT) was performed and showed “no acute intracranial process.” What would be the most helpful measure to confirm the diagnosis?

options.A: Computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the brain
options.B: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of the brain
options.D: MRA (magnetic resonance angiography) of the brain

explanation: This is a classic presentation for pituitary apoplexy, or hemorrhage into the pituitary with sudden pituitary expansion. Most cases of pituitary apoplexy occur due to hemorrhage into a pituitary adenoma. MRI of the brain is the imaging study of choice for optimal visualization of the chiasm to make this diagnosis. CTA or MRA would be the study of choice to look for an aneurysm which in theory could cause a right pupil involving 3rd nerve palsy and a left 6th nerve palsy due to increased intracranial pressure but would be unlikely to cause a symmetric bitemporal hemianopia (typically causes asymmetric visual field deficits because it is not a midline structure). EMG is one study used to evaluate for myasthenia gravis (MG) and is always good to consider in any extraocular motility deficit (especially bilateral deficits). MG does not cause headache and would not result in a bitemporal hemianopia. A CT of the head is quick, easy to obtain, and can diagnosis pituitary apoplexy but is not sufficiently sensitive to rule out the diagnosis. By far the best imaging study for evaluation of the sellar / parasellar region of the pituitary, cavernous sinus, and optic chiasm is an MRI. question: A 60-year-old patient comes in with vague visual complaints over the last 5 years. His visual acuity is 20/25 OU but your confrontation exam is abnormal in both eyes. A Humphrey visual field is performed and the results are displayed above. Which of the following would be the most likely to result in these visual field defects?
explanation: Occasionally standardized tests will ask simple questions in an unfamiliar fashion. These questions can be frustrating because the test taker knows the material but simply misinterpreted the question. This is an example of such a question. If a question seems really easy then stop for a moment and re-read it to see if you can identify a trick. Most people know that glaucoma commonly causes binasal visual field deficits but the fields in this question were NOT presented "from the patient's perspective" so that at first glance there appears to be a bitemporal superior quadranopia. Some may wonder why a glaucomatous visual field defect would appear to abide by the vertical midline. A closer examination shows that the visual field defect in the left eye does not actually abide by the vertical midline. The visual field defect in the right eye does mostly abide by the vertical midline but sometimes glaucomatous defects can give this illusion. If the field was repeated in the right eye 2 years later and we presume glaucomatous progression, the pattern would have more of a superior arcuate appearance. Binasal deficits from central nervous system disease are exceedingly rare (case reportable). Pituitary adenomas classically cause bitemporal defects that are greater superiorly due to compression of the chiasm inferiorly. Craniopharyngiomas generally cause bitemporal defects that are greater inferiorly because they usually arise from above the chiasm and compress the superior aspect of the chiasm. Also among chiasmal compressive lesions in a 60-year-old male, pituitary adenoma would be more common than a craniopharyngioma. Occipital lobe strokes classically cause a contralateral homonymous hemianopia with or without macular sparing. Patients with which mitochondrial DNA point mutation responsible for Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) are the most likely to show late spontaneous improvement in visual function? A.11778 B.14484 C.3460 D.5780 High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: The rate of spontaneous late visual recovery in the 14484 mutation is about 65% as opposed to only 4% in the more common 11778 mutation A 23-year old with a recent history of acute myelogenous leukemia presents with sudden vision loss in the right eye for one day. The examination of his left eye is normal. Examination of his right eye reveals hand motions vision, an afferent pupillary defect (APD) OD, and a pale swollen optic nerve with a lumpy, nodular appearance. What is the next most appropriate step? A.Call a radiation oncology consult and order an MRI orbits STAT B.Start IV acyclovir immediately C.Order a chest / abdomen / pelvis CT D.Order a STAT OCT of the optic nerve High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: This is a classic presentation for leukemic / lymphomatous infiltration of the optic nerve. Typically, patients have a known history of leukemia or lymphoma although optic nerve infiltration may be the presenting sign. The treatment most promising for vision recovery is focal radiation treatment to the involved optic nerve head. IV acyclovir would be an appropriate treatment for severe herpetic infection which can occur in immunocompromised hosts but there is no reason to suspect that in this case. An OCT of the optic nerve head will surely show abnormal findings of nerve head swelling and possibly a mass lesion in this case but will only serve to delay the definitive management required (radiation). A pan-CT of the chest / abdomen / pelvis might be a consideration for AML staging but would typically be ordered by the oncologist and would not taking precedence over the definitive treatment of radiation to the optic nerve heads. A 60-year-old patient presents with a homonymous heminanopsia, but with normal visual acuity. Which of the following is the most common cause of this visual field defect in an adult? A.neoplasm B.trauma C.ischemic stroke D.hemorrhage High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: While the cause is usually ischemic stroke, any patient found to have a previously undiagnosed homonymous hemianopia on routine exam must have neuro-imaging for further evaluation (preferably an MRI). Often these patients will complain of blurred vision in one eye on the side of the homonymous hemianopia instead of realizing that the vision loss is actually in both eyes. The most common cause of unilateral retrochiasmal visual loss (i.e. which would produce a homonymous hemianopsia) in adults is a stroke (~60% of cases). The other major causes of this visual field defect in adults is from trauma (~10%) and hemorrhage (~10%). In contrast, the most common cause of retrochiasmal visual loss in children is from trauma and tumors (or the surgical resection necessary for their removal). A lesion of the right optic tract might be expected to result in what finding? A.an afferent pupillary defect (APD) in the left eye B.an afferent pupillary defect (APD) in the right eye C.a right homonymous hemianopia (in both eyes) D.a left hemianopia in the right eye only High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Optic tract lesions classically result in a contralateral homonymous hemianopia (often incongruous) and a contralateral afferent pupillary defect. The APD is contralateral to the lesion because each tract contains more crossed than uncrossed pupillary fibers (recall there is an asymmetric decussation of all axons at the chiasm). Therefore, a lesion of the optic tract will cause more damage to fibers crossing from the contralateral eye than uncrossed fibers from the ipsilateral eye. which of the following is not a known cause of infiltrative optic neuropathy? A.lymphoma B.sarcoidosis C.varicella zoster virus (VZV) D.tuberculosis (TB) High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: Infiltrative optic neuropathy often presents acutely with devastating effects on optic nerve function (visual fields and visual acuity). Causes include optic nerve gliomas, leukemia, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, syphilis, TB, fungal infections and meningeal carcinomatosis. When VZV affects optic nerve function (often referred to as "orbital zoster") it is thought to be a vasculitis that cuts off arterial circulation to the optic nerve. Often, there are preceding or concurrent VZV skin vesicles and/or diffuse unilateral motility deficits from hypoxia of the extraocular muscles. A neurologist refers a patient to you who has been newly diagnosed with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS). The neurologist wishes to start the oral medication, fingolimod (brand name: Gilenya™), as an alternative to intramuscular interferon beta-1a injections. What ocular side effect may occur with fingolimod? A.increased rate of optic neuritis B.non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy C.multiple cranial nerve palsies D.macular edema High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: D Explanation: Daily oral fingolimod demonstrated superior efficacy in the treatment of relapsing-remitting MS compared to weekly intramuscular injections of interferon beta-1a in a prospective, randomized controlled trial (N Engl J Med. 2010;362:402-15). The annualized relapse rate was lower in the fingolimod groups compared to interferon beta-1a and the MRI results corroborated these results. The only adverse ocular finding was the presence of macular edema in <1% of patients receiving fingolimod. This macular edema occurred within 4 months of receiving this medication and was asymptomatic in half of these affected patients. Which of the following tests is the most appropriate to assess if a patient's chronic vision loss may be due to an old branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) involving the macula which occured 5 years prior? A.Visual evoked potential (VEP) B.Full field electroretinogram (ERG) C.Potential acuity meter (PAM) D.Multifocal electroretinogram (mfERG) High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: A chronic branch retinal artery occlusion often shows no detectable fundoscopy findings and may have a completely normal appearing fluorescein angiography. A VEP is rarely useful clinically and only shows gross deficits anywhere along the afferent visual pathway from the macula to the occipital lobe. An abnormal VEP cannot localize the site of pathology within the visual pathway. The PAM is used to assess macular vision potential through hazy media (usually a cataract). A full field ERG is best at evaluating rod function although the stimulus frequency can be altered to evaluate gross cone function. For assessing focal retinal dysfunction within the macula, such as a small BRAO, multifocal ERG is most useful. What is the most common hereditary optic neuropathy? A.autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA) B.Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) C.Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD) D.Behr syndrome High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: ADOA (or Kjer's syndrome) is the most common hereditary optic neuropathy with an estimated incidence of 1 in 50,000. About 50-70% of patients with the ADOA phenotype have a mutation in the OPA1 gene on chromosome 3. The OPA1 gene codes for a GTPase that appears to have a function in mitochondrial energy production and maintenance of mitochondrial membrane integrity. LHON is a maternally-inherited disease of mitochondrial dysfunction caused by point mutations in mitochondrial DNA. Wolfram syndrome is a syndrome with a unique constellation of findings including diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, and sensorineural deafness. It is generally inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion (though can be sporadic). Behr syndrome is a variant of autosomal recessive optic atrophy associated with other neurologic abnormalities including ataxia, pyramidal and extrapyramidal dysfunction, hypertonia, intellectual disability, urinary incontinence, and pes cavus. Experts believe Behr syndrome is likely a wastebasket for many different undiagnosed diseases (and is unlikely to show up on your test). Autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA) has all of the following characteristics EXCEPT: A.insidious bilateral vision loss over years B.known pathogenic mutations in the OPA1 gene of chromosome 3 C.focal temporal excavation of involved optic nerves D.nerve fiber bundle type visual field defects respecting the horizontal meridian High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: ADOA typically presents in the first 10 years of life but can present much later. Patients with ADOA often offer a vague family history of color blindness, progressive glaucoma, or poor vision of unknown etiology in close family members which supports the dominant inheritance (although may be a de novo mutation). Vision is typically 20/60-20/200 upon diagnosis with many patients not realizing they have a problem until obtaining a routine eye exam. Color vision is generally diminished and old literature suggests tritanopia is most characteristic of ADOA (although more recent literature found color vision deficits of all types). The optic nerves have a characteristic temporal excavation with pallor in about half of cases and diffuse pallor in other cases. Visual fields typically show central / cecocentral depression although some demonstrate global depression. Neuro-imaging of the brain / orbits should be performed prior to the diagnosis of ADOA to rule out compressive lesions. n 18-year-old girl presents to your clinic as a referral from her optometrist for "bilateral disc swelling." The patient's only complaint is a new-onset, mild headache starting 3 weeks ago. Her medical history is significant for acne vulgaris for which she is taking isotretinoin. Her visual acuity is 20/20 OU, her pupillary exam is normal, she has full ductions and versions, and her static perimetry is full OU. Her dilated exam is shown above. Which of the following represents the next best course of management? A.acetaminophen or a NSAID for her mild headaches B.oral acetazolamide for her mild headaches C.lumbar puncture D.MRI / MRV High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The fundus photo depicts bilateral disc edema with tortuous retinal vessels OU. There is perhaps a peripapillary hemorrhage at 7 o'clock on the right optic disc as well as some obscuration of the vessels as they pass over the disc rim. The differential diagnosis of disc edema can be broken down according to the most frequent causes: • Most common: papilledema, optic neuritis, anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, pseudopapilledema • Somewhat common: CRVO, diabetic papillopathy • Uncommon: posterior uveitis, hypotony, malignant hypertension, Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy, optic nerve infiltration (e.g. sarcoidosis, lymphoma) This patient most likely has papilledema given the appearance of her discs, her relatively-intact visual function, her headache symptoms, and lack of other symptoms (e.g. no pain on eye movement). As you know, the basic definition of papilledema is optic disc swelling caused by increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Though this clinical vignette wants you to jump to the diagnosis of pseudotumor cerebri, you MUST get neuro-imaging to exclude other causes of papilledema. These other causes include an intracranial tumor, hydrocephalus, intracranial hemorrhage, meningitis, and venous thrombosis. Though CT with contrast is sometimes used, MRI of the brain is preferred since it is more sensitive for detecting the various causes of increased ICP. MRV is also typically performed at the same time due to its convenience and ability to help rule-in/out venous sinus thrombosis. Finally, it is important to note that this patient is taking isotretinoin which is a vitamin A derivative medication and is a known cause of intracranial hypertension. In this case the work- up for probable papilledema needs to be completed but you would also want to stop isotretinoin. A patient has his right eye pharmacologically dilated while his left eye remains undilated. Assume that he has a known longstanding right afferent pupillary defect from prior exams. You know that to properly assess for a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) you must hold a light indirectly on the _______ eye while a direct light is swung back and forth between the eyes. In this particular case the ______ pupil will dilate when direct light is swung from the _______ eye to the _______ eye. A.left; left; right; left B.left; left; left; right C.right; left; left; right D.It is not possible to assess for a RAPD in this scenario Neuro-ophthalmology High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Dilation of one eye does not prevent the accurate assessment of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). If one eye is dilated, simply hold a dim indirect light source to the side of the undilated eye (in this case the left eye) and perform the swinging flashlight test. If the undilated eye has a RAPD then it will dilate as expected when the flashlight is swung over from the dilated eye. If the dilated eye has a RAPD, the undilated eye will dilate when the flashlight is swung from the undilated eye to the dilated eye. Some refer to this as checking for a RAPD "by reverse" but others object to the use of this terminology calling it a misnomer. Misnomer or not, most ophthalmologists understand what is meant by assessing a RAPD "by reverse." Which of the following medications has been implicated as a cause of intracranial hypertension? A.cyclosporine B.furosemide (Lasix) C.sildenafil (Viagra) D.escitalopram (Lexapro) High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: It is important to know the medicines that are associated with drug-induced intracranial hypertension. The more commonly implicated drugs include: vitamin A and vitamin A derivatives (isotretinoin), the tetracycline family of antibiotics, cyclosporine, oral contraceptives, prednisone (both the use and sudden withdrawal), and synthetic growth hormone. Lasix is actually a second-line treatment for IIH patients. Viagra has a questionable association with non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy. A 75-year-old male with a history of heavy alcohol and cigarette use comes to your clinic today with a 2-month history of progressive visual loss in both eyes to 20/100 best corrected with associated prominent photopsias in both eyes. Exam one month ago by an outside ophthalmologist found 20/50 vision in both eyes with global depression on a reliable 24-2 Humphrey visual field. An electroretinogram (ERG) was performed a week ago and showed marked reduction in amplitude of both rod and cone function. Aside from his vision and mild vitritis OU, his ocular exam today is unremarkable (including normal pupils and fundus OU). What would be the next best step in diagnosis of this patient? A.optic nerve optical coherence tomography (OCT) B.thyroid function studies C.CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis D.fluorescein angiography (FA) High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient has a classic presentation for cancer-associated retinopathy (CAR) although melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR) is also a definite consideration. CAR and MAR are both paraneoplastic, acquired retinal syndromes which share many similar features including progressive vision loss with photopsias and nyctalopia. Both diseases often have normal fundus findings until late in the disease course when retinal arterioles may become attenuated with thinning of the RPE and atrophy of the optic nerve. CAR tends to present with both Cone And Rod retinal dysfunction (cone > rod) and MAR Mostly Affects Rods although either can affect rods and/or cones (shout out to OQ user "Grimlock" for that memory aid. A late onset acquired retinal rod or cone dysfunction on ERG is highly suggestive of CAR or MAR. Vitritis (often mild as in this case) may or may not be present on exam in either MAR and CAR- both have been reported in the literature but vitritis is not required for the diagnosis. About 50% of patients with CAR have a known diagnosis of cancer at onset of ocular disease while the vast majority of MAR patients have a known history of melanoma at onset. The most common inciting malignancy in CAR is small cell carcinoma of the lung although other carcinomas of the lungs, breast, uterus, and cervix have also been associated. While new generation OCTs of the macula may show non-specific pathologic changes of the outer retina with CAR / MAR, an OCT of the optic nerve would expected to be normal in CAR / MAR and would not prove useful in this case. Patients with thyroid associated ophthalmopathy (TAO) usually show signs of either eyelid retraction, eye muscle motility disturbance, strabismus, or proptosis on exam AND thyroid function tests can be low, high, or normal in patients with TAO so it is only a marginally useful test. A FA would not be expected to show any abnormalities that would aid diagnosis in this patient. An 80-year-old Veteran who enjoys his cigarettes, rum, and junk food presents with visual decline in both eyes over 1 year with an objective decline in serial measurements of VA and color vision bilaterally. Both eyes show a similar visual field and optic nerve appearance. In the context of a normal macular exam, which optic nerve appearance (A-D) would you expect in this patient with the visual field shown above? A.Image A B.Image B C.Image C D.Image D High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The visual field presented is a Humphrey automated 24-2 visual field of the left eye demonstrating a cecocentral scotoma. Of the pictures shown, image D showing mild to moderate temporal pallor would correspond best to this visual field defect and history strongly suggestive of a combined nutritional optic neuropathy and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Temporal pallor is a very non-specific sign of damage to the optic nerve and is associated with many different types of visual field defects from damage to the optic nerve but is the typical appearance associated with nutritional and tobacco / alcohol amblyopia. Generally this causes relatively symmetric bilateral central / cecocentral vision loss due to loss of the papillomacular bundle causing temporal atrophy of the optic nerve. While we all like clean diagnoses (e.g. vitamin B-12 deficiency or copper deficiency) many patients with this type of optic neuropathy have a "dirty diagnosis" full of both poisons (smoking and drinking) and vitamin deficiency from poor nutrition leading to mitochondrial failure of the retinal ganglion cells of the papillomacular bundle. Image A shows a normal optic nerve head with a small cup-to-disc ratio (“disc at risk”). A disc at risk without swelling or pallor is not associated with any visual field defect. Image B shows a severely swollen, hyperemic optic nerve with surrounding exudates that would be typical for a patient presenting with increased intracranial pressure (i.e. papilledema) (e.g. from pseudotumor cerebri, compressive tumor, or venous sinus thrombosis). Papilledema does not typically cause a cecocentral scotoma. Instead it causes enlarged blind spots and glaucomatous type field defects. End stage severe papilledema, like end-stage glaucoma, can cause central vision loss once the periphery is lost. Image C shows a glaucomatous optic nerve with prominent cupping and a focal notch at about 5 o’clock. Glaucoma is classically associated with nerve fiber layer type defects such as nasal steps, arcuate defects, and altitudinal defects. It would be highly atypical for an optic nerve with prominent glaucomatous cupping and notching of the neuro-retinal rim to demonstrate an isolated cecocentral visual field defect. According to the Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial, what is the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement in patients with acute monocular non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy? A.1-2% B.12-19% C.25-35% D.50-60% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: This is a fact that must be memorized. For comparison, the rate of contralateral involvement in patients with untreated monocular vision loss from arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy due to giant cell arteritis is estimated to be 54-95% within weeks. OQ users have been frustrated by apparently different statistics in different "reputable sources" regarding the risk of contralateral NAION in a patient who suffers unilateral NAION. The current neuro BCSC states that "the 5-year risk of contralateral involvement is 15%." This is based on very good data from the ischemic optic neuropathy decompression trial follow-up study which found the rate to be 14.7% in 5 years.1 Different statistics quoted by review manuals may be looking at lifetime risk (rather than 5 year risk) or may be quoting smaller studies. OQ has researched this topic thoroughly and we are sticking with the current BCSC text on this question. Don't send us hateful comments if your review manual has a different statistic. 1Newman NJ, Scherer R, Langenberg P, Kelman S, Feldon S, Kaufman D, Dickersin K; Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial Research Group. What is the term for vision which deteriorates in brighter light? A.hemeralopia B.photophobia C.metamorphopsia D.palinopsia High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Photophobia is a "fear of light" or sensitivity to light. While closely related to hemeralopia, or deterioration of vision in higher light environments, it is not the same. Hemeralopia is often described in patients with cone dystrophy. Metamorphopsia is a distortion of vision where straight objects appear wavy or crooked. Metamorphopsia typically is described by patients with macular disease. Palinopsia is an illusion marked by the preservation of images or "afterimages." Palinopsia can occur as an isolated visual phenomenon or in association with medications, hallucinogenic drugs, seizure disorders, and/or visual pathway lesions. A 60-year old male with no past ocular history undergoes a 6-hour cardiac bypass surgery. When he awakes from surgery he is found to have hand motion vision in both eyes. Aside from his abnormal vision, sluggish pupillary function, and pupillary light-near dissociation, his exam is unremarkable (including his dilated fundus exam). What is the most likely diagnosis? A.Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy B.Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy C.Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy D.Dorsal midbrain syndrome High Yield: No Your Answer: A Correct Answer: A Explanation: Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy (PION) is much rarer than anterior ischemic optic neuropathy but similarly is believed to be related to hypoperfusion of the posterior optic nerve. Usually the hypoperfusion is due to a perfect storm of contributing risk factors including anemia, hypotension, poor cardiac output, hypovolemia, and cardiopulmonary instability during surgery. Rarely PION can be related to a vasculitic process including giant cell arteritis, lupus-associated vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa, and VZV related vasculitis. Unlike anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, PION almost always has a normal appearing optic nerve in the acute phase. Dorsal midbrain syndrome does include pupillary light-near dissociation, but has other findings not exhibited in this patient and does not typically result in sudden bilateral vision loss. As an aside, any disease process causing bilateral optic neuropathy can result in pupillary light-near dissociation. A 22-year-old African American female presents with vision loss in the left eye over the past 2 days. She reports severe left eye pain that is worse with eye movement. Her examination shows 20/20 vision in the right eye and 20/25 vision in the left eye. She has normal color vision, alignment, IOP, and motility. Her pupils show a left afferent pupillary defect. Her right eye exam is essentially normal. Confrontation fields are diffusely constricted in the left eye. Slit lamp exam shows 2+ anterior chamber cell and moderate optic nerve swelling in the left eye. An MRI of the orbits with IV contrast is performed and shown above. What type of optic neuropathy does this patient have? A.Demyelinating optic neuritis B.Ischemic optic neuropathy C.Optic perineuritis D.Nutritional optic neuropathy High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: The image shows a coronal section of a T1-weighted, fat-saturated post-contrast MRI. The MRI shows marked enhancement and slight thickening of the optic nerve sheath while the optic nerve itself shows very little enhancement. Optic nerve sheath enhancement can be seen in optic nerve sheath meningiomas and optic perineuritis (OPN). This patient’s acute presentation and pain with eye movement is suggestive of optic perineuritis. Defined by inflammation of the meninges surrounding the optic nerve, OPN is a radiologic and pathologic diagnosis. The era of MRI has enabled increased recognition of this entity while in the past these cases may have been categorized as “optic neuritis” or “atypical optic neuritis.” OPN is generally considered on the spectrum of orbital pseudotumor because in many cases there is concomitant orbital inflammation and like orbital pseudotumor it is usually idiopathic inflammation. Additional known etiologies of OPN, however, include sarcoidosis, giant cell arteritis, lymphoma, Wegener’s granulomatosis, tuberculosis and syphilis. Without the MRI to aide in the diagnosis of OPN, it is virtually indistinguishable from demyelinating optic neuritis (DON). In contrast to DON, OPN has a reported slight tendency to less commonly involve the central visual field, often occurs alongside other radiographic and clinical findings of orbital inflammation, and is exquisitely steroid responsive. As we alluded to above, reasons to distinguish OPN from DON is that OPN: 1) Does not carry the same risk of future multiple sclerosis as DON; and 2) Requires a laboratory evaluation to rule-out other causes such as sarcoidosis, giant cell arteritis, lymphoma, Wegener’s granulomatosis, tuberculosis and syphilis. Ingestion of which of the following substances causes an acute, bilateral toxic optic neuropathy with associated severe vision loss and disc edema? A.Ethambutol B.Ethanol C.Chloramphenicol D.Methanol High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: Chronic use of ethambutol, ethanol, chloramphenicol, hydroxyquinolones, penicillamine, cisplatin, and vincristine are associated with chronic toxic optic neuropathy. Chronic toxic optic neuropathy and chronic nutritional neuropathy from B-12 / folate / thiamine classically result in diminished central visual acuity from central / cecocentral scotomas with selective loss of the papillomacular nerve fiber layer and optic nerve pallor. Methanol and ethylene glycol toxicity, however, occurs immediately with ingestion and results in devastating acute, diffuse vision loss with associated disc edema. Which of the following would be expected to result in a left afferent pupillary defect? A.A right optic nerve lesion B.A right optic tract lesion C.A right optic radiation lesion D.A right-sided lesion of the primary visual cortex High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: A lesion of the optic tract often results in an afferent pupillary defect of the contralateral eye. This is thought to occur because there are more crossed than uncrossed pupillary fibers in the optic tract. A lesion of the right optic tract results in decreased afferent input from both retinas but relatively-speaking there is a more marked reduction of afferent input from the contralateral eye. This is a simple concept yet often trips students up. A 22-year-old African American female presents with vision loss in the left eye over the past 2 days. She reports severe left eye pain that is worse with eye movement. Her examination shows 20/20 vision in the right eye and 20/25 vision in the left eye. Confrontation fields are diffusely constricted in the left eye. Slit lamp exam shows 2+ anterior chamber cell and moderate optic nerve swelling in the left eye. An MRI of the orbits with IV contrast is performed and shown above. What would NOT be considered in the differential for this patient’s optic neuropathy? A.Demyelinating optic neuritis associated with multiple sclerosis B.Granulomatosis with polyangiitis C.Syphilis D.Sarcoidosis High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The image shows a coronal section of a T1-weighted, fat-saturated post-contrast MRI.
