question: A patient comes to you as a second opinion with limited medical records from her prior care providers. Which of the following findings or symptoms would make you question the diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension in a 30-year-old obese female with bilateral disc edema on examination and a two-year history of headaches?
explanation: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) frequently presents with severe headaches, nausea/vomiting, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations (lasting seconds), and *horizontal* binocular diplopia due to cranial nerve VI dysfunction from increased intracranial pressure. Typical exam findings include papilledema (present in over 90%), enlargement of the blind spot (present in most patients with papilledema), glaucoma-like visual field defects, and cranial nerve VI palsy (can be unilateral or bilateral). Pulsatile tinnitus is a nonspecific symptoms of elevated intracranial pressure and is very common with IIH. *Vertical* binocular diplopia would suggest possible impairment of either cranial nerve III or IV and should not occur in IIH. There are case reports of cranial nerve III or IV impairment associated with IIH but they are very few. Aside from cranial nerve VI dysfunction, any other cranial nerve deficits should raise serious doubts about the diagnosis of IIH and prompt further evaluation. According to the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT), which of the following was found to be a benefit of IV methylprednisolone followed by PO prednisone in the treatment of optic neuritis? A.Faster visual recovery in the affected eye B.Improved visual acuity outcome in the affected eye C.Improved visual field outcome in the affected eye D.A reduced risk of multiple sclerosis (MS) development at 10 years High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The ONTT showed that IV corticosteroid treatment (methylprednisolone 250 mg every 6 hours x 3 days) followed by oral prednisone (1 mg / kg / day x 11 days) resulted in a quicker recovery by 1-2 weeks but did not change long-term outcome compared to placebo. It did find that IV followed by PO steroids reduced the rate of progression to MS for the first 2 years in high risk patients with 2 or more suspicious white matter lesions on MRI. By 3 years after the initial event, however, this effect diminished to become equivalent to placebo. Oral prednisone alone in the treatment of optic neuritis was found to nearly double the rate of recurrent optic neuritis compared to placebo and the IV steroid / PO steroid treatment group. For that reason, oral steroids alone are never utilized in the treatment of an initial bout of optic neuritis. There is no good data on the treatment of oral steroids for subsequent bouts of optic neuritis. Most neuro- ophthalmologists extrapolate from the ONTT data, however, and choose to abstain from using prednisone alone for the treatment of optic neuritis. A 25-year-old type I diabetic with poor blood sugar control (last HgbA1c = 9.5) presents as a referral from his optometrist after bilateral disc edema was found on routine examination. His vision is 20/25 OU and exam is remarkable for moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy and moderate disc edema bilaterally with fine disc surface telangiectatic vessels. What other finding on history or exam would dissuade you from the diagnosis of diabetic papillopathy? A.the absence of an afferent pupillary defect (APD) B.leakage from the optic disc telangiectasias on fluorescein angiography (FA) C.superior arcuate visual field defects on Humphrey visual field (HVF) testing OU D.no subjective visual complaints High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: Diabetic papillopathy is usually a mild optic neuropathy with minimal visual manifestations. While it is was originally described in type 1 diabetics, it is considered to be more common in older type 2 diabetics. The exact mechanism is unknown but thought to be due to ischemia of the optic nerve head with resultant swelling. Typically, it resolves in 2-10 months with minimal optic nerve damage and ultimately visual acuity outcome depends more on the extent of concomitant diabetic retinopathy than optic nerve pathology. Visual fields may show enlargement of the blind spot but should not show any other major defects (if other defects are present the diagnosis is highly unlikely). The optic disc may have telangiectasias on the surface which look similar to neovascularization of the disc (NVD) and often leak on FA. Unlike NVD, however, these telangiectasias should not be seen rising into the vitreous or leaking into the vitreous on FA. When bilateral diabetic papillopathy appears to be present, neuro-imaging and a lumbar puncture should be performed to rule out papilledema. Which of the following is not associated with acute optic disc edema? A.impaired axoplasmic flow in ganglion cell axons B.chorioretinal folds C.macular edema D.loss of the capillary net on the optic disc surface High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Optic disc edema can occur from any process which hinders axoplasmic flow in ganglion cells including optic nerve compression, increased intracranial pressure, ischemia, and inflammation. Findings associated with disc edema include an elevated appearance of the optic nerve head, blurring of the optic nerve head margins and blood vessels as they traverse the border of the optic nerve due to nerve fiber layer edema, retinal venous dilation and tortuosity, peripapillary hemorrhages and exudates, macular edema and chorioretinal folds. Loss of disc surface capillaries is a finding of optic nerve atrophy and acute optic disc edema actually causes prominent "hyperemic" vasculature of the optic nerve head. Which of the following features favors the diagnosis of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy as opposed to arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy? A.a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.4 in the contralateral eye B.pallid swelling of the affected optic nerve C.patchy choroidal filling on fluorescein angiography (FA) in the affected eye D.visual acuity better than 20/200 in the affected eye High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The most important first step in diagnosis of patients with anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is distinguishing the cases of arteritic (from giant cell arteritis) from non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is often more visually-devastating than its non-arteritic counterpart with 60% of patients with less than 20/200 vision. GCA damages vision by vasculitic occlusion of the posterior ciliary arteries that supply the optic nerve head and choroid; therefore, it is common to see "pallid" disc edema due to severe ischemia along with patchy choroidal filling on FA in the affected eye (and sometimes even the seemingly unaffected contralateral eye). Optic disc swelling can make it difficult to judge a patient's baseline cup-to-disc ratio in the affected eye prior to the ischemic event. Based on the fact that most people have symmetric optic nerves, a small cup-to-disc ratio in the contralateral eye is suggestive of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy in the affected eye. How long after injury to the retinal ganglion cells or their axons does it take for optic nerve atrophy to appear? A.1-2 days B.1-2 weeks C.4-6 weeks D.10-12 weeks High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: This fact simply needs to be memorized. Optic atrophy does not occur in the acute phase of optic nerve or retinal damage but rather requires 4-6 weeks to appear. Optic atrophy will occur with significant damage, ranging from the retina to the lateral geniculate body, where the majority of retinal ganglion cells synapse. Of the tests provided, which of the following tests would be the best test to distinguish between arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy and non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy? A.Spectral domain OCT B.ERG C.Humphrey visual field D.Fluorescein angiography High Yield: Yes Your Answer: A Correct Answer: D Explanation: While CRP, ESR, platelet counts, and a detailed history often help in making the diagnosis of arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy due to giant cell arteritis (GCA), a fluorescein angiography (FA) can also be a very useful test. While non-arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy likely stems from diminished perfusion to the optic nerve head, artertic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy is due to a vasculitis of posterior ciliary arteries supplying the optic nerve head and the adjacent choroid. Therefore, cases of arteritic ischemic optic neuropathy often demonstrate patchy choroidal perfusion on FA. Occasionally patients with vision loss from GCA may infarct a posterior ciliary artery that does not supply the optic nerve head in which case the patient may have vision loss with a completely normal fundus exam. In that scenario the vision loss would not be due to arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy but rather choroidal ischemia / infarction. The fundus photo and FA series below is an excellent example of what that would look like. Notice the large dark region devoid of choroidal filling temporally despite normal filling of the nasal choroid, cilio- retinal artery, and retinal vasculature. In the correct clinical context, this FA finding is highly suggestive of GCA (and high yield for standardized tests).

question: Approximately how much (measured posteriorly from the anterior tip) of the temporal lobe can be resected without causing a visual field deficit?
explanation: The optic radiations extend from the lateral geniculate nucleus to the ipsilateral primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. The fibers corresponding to the contralateral superior quadrant visual field from both eyes pass anteriorly into the temporal lobe in a path known as the "loop of Meyer". This becomes important when neurosurgeons excise tissue from the temporal lobe because depending on how much tissue is excised, surgery may cause a contralateral "pie in the sky" type visual field defect by violating the loop of Meyer. s a general rule of retro-chiasmal optic pathway pathology (lesions located posterior to the optic chiasm), which of the following is true? A.More anteriorly-located lesions result in monocular visual field deficits. B.More posteriorly-located lesions result in monocular visual field deficits. C.More anteriorly-located lesions result in more congruous visual field deficits. D.More posteriorly-located lesions result in more congruous visual field deficits. High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Unilateral pathology posterior to the chiasm ("retro-chiasmal") virtually always results in binocular visual field deficits. The one exception to this rule is that in theory a small occipital lobe lesion in the far anterior aspect of the primary visual cortex could result in a contralateral loss of the far temporal crescent. This far temporal crescent of the visual field is located 60-90 degrees from fixation and projects to only the contralateral occipital lobe. Otherwise, it is a general rule that a more posteriorly located lesion of the retro-chiasmal optic pathways is more likely to result in a congruous visual field deficit. A congruous visual field defect is one in which the deficits in each corresponding hemifield are very similar. Occipital lobe lesions, therefore, are more likely to result in a congruous (or similar) contralateral hemianopia (in both eyes). A parietal lobe lesion, however, may result in an incongruous hemianopia where one eye has a complete hemi-field cut and the other eye has only partial hemi-field loss. This is not a strict rule but rather describes a tendency. There are plenty of exceptions to this "rule." A 70-year-old male presents for consideration of strabismus surgery. explanation: The lesion is an arachnoid cyst located in the left cavernous sinus. Arachnoid cysts are typically primary developmental cysts due to splitting of the arachnoid membrane in utero resulting in a potential space for cerebrospinal fluid collection. Cysts rarely cause isolated cranial nerve palsies but may if located in the correct region. The image shows a T2 hyperintense lesion in the medial cavernous sinus. The cavernous sinus is one of the dural venous sinuses and receives venous drainage from the orbit. The important structures and nerves that transverse the cavernous sinus are highlighted in the image. A lesion that involves the cavernous sinus is suggested by a combination of unilateral third, fourth, or sixth nerve dysfunction and hypoesthesia of the face and cornea in the region of V1 and V2. A Horner syndrome may also be caused due to sympathetic disruption, as the sympathetic fibers destined for the iris dilator run posteriorly with the sixth nerve in the cavernous sinus before joining the nasocillary branch of V1 more anteriorly. Additionally, venous drainage from the orbit can be disrupted leading to orbital signs of venous congestion such as chemosis, conjunctival injection, and proptosis. This can be the case with large mass lesions, acute pituitary apoplexy, thrombosis of the cavernous sinus, infection, and carotid-cavernous fistulas. The majority of cavernous sinus findings are due to a mass lesion. Other lesions on the differential include trauma, cavernous sinus thrombosis, infection, carotid-cavernous fistula, and intercavernous aneurysms. If only one cranial nerve is involved from a cavernous sinus lesion, it is usually the sixth nerve as this is the only nerve that runs medially through the cavernous sinus and is not protected by the lateral dural wall. Additionally, the lesion in this patient is in the medial aspect of the sinus making involvement of the sixth nerve most likely. WRONG ANSWERS: • (Choice B): If only one cranial nerve is involved from a cavernous sinus lesion, it is usually the sixth nerve as this is the only nerve that runs medially through the cavernous sinus and is not protected by the lateral dural wall. Additionally, the lesion in this patient is in the medial aspect of the sinus making involvement of the sixth nerve most likely. • (Choice C): The optic nerve does not transverse the cavernous sinus. The orbital apex (anterior to the cavernous sinus) contains the optic, third, fourth, sixth, and V1 nerves. A lesion of the orbital apex can present similarly to those of the cavernous sinus. Optic nerve dysfunction and lack of V2 involvement can distinguish the two entities. • (Choice D): The mandibular division of the fifth nerve (V3 division) does not transverse the cavernous sinus. V3 innervates the skin of the jaw and has motor fibers for the muscles of mastication and the neck. Which of the following ocular findings is most likely to result in binocular diplopia (assuming no other ocular pathology is present)? A.Epiretinal membrane B.Cataract C.Dry eye D.Uncorrected corneal astigmatism High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: All of the answer choices above are known causes of monocular diplopia. The term monocular diplopia is often used by ophthalmologists and patients frequently complain of monocular “double vision.” Most of the time when patients complain of monocular double vision, they more specifically notice subtle ghosting of image margins rather than two distinct images. Epiretinal membrane (ERM) is an unusual example of an intraocular finding that can result in binocular diplopia. ERM can cause binocular diplopia by dragging the fovea in the affected eye (sometimes referred to as “dragged fovea syndrome”). When the fovea has been dragged from its usual position, the retinal periphery of both eyes and the fovea of both eyes are no longer aligned when looking at a visual target. The retinal periphery exerts greater influence on binocular image fusion than the fovea. Thus, once a fovea has been dragged from its physiologic location, the retinal periphery of both eyes will continue to fuse but the images seen by both foveas cannot be fused. As a result of the underlying pathophysiology, prisms are notoriously ineffective in relieving diplopia in these patients. ERM peeling can be attempted in these cases although it is often ineffective in relieving binocular diplopia given that the dragged fovea usually does not return to its physiologic location.

question: Exam demonstrates corrected visual acuities of 20/20 OD, 20/100 OS with eccentric fixation, equal and reactive pupils with a 3+ APD OS, and intraocular pressures of 21 OD and 23 OS. Fundoscopic exam demonstrates sharp nerves, a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.3 and temporal pallor OU. Visual field testing is shown. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s symptoms?
explanation: This pattern of visual field loss is consistent with a junctional scotoma, which is classically caused by anterior chiasmal compression. This visual field pattern is comprised of the following: • An ipsilateral central scotoma or diffuse visual field loss caused by a lesion compressing the ipsilateral optic nerve anterior to the chiasm. • A contralateral superior temporal defect due to compression of decussating optic nerve fibers from the contralateral inferonasal retina, which represent the supratemporal visual field. After decussation, these fibers run approximately 4 mm anteriorly into the ipsilateral optic nerve before they reverse course and travel posteriorly to enter the optic tract. These fibers are termed “Wilbrand’s Knee”. The most common cause of chiasmal compression is a pituitary adenoma. Approximately 30% of pituitary adenomas are nonfunctioning and these patients will typically present with visual complaints and generalized headaches. In addition, compression of the pituitary gland can cause hyposecretion of TSH, LH/FSH, ACTH and other hormones leading to symptoms of fatigue and lethargy. These symptoms are nonspecific and are usually only picked up on review of systems. Tumors that actively secrete hormones, on the other hand, are typically detected prior to visual complaints due to the systemic endocrine symptoms. In which of the following scenarios would optociliary shunt vessels most likely be seen? A.a 40-year old with poorly controlled pseudotumor cerebri for 10 years B.a 10-year old with an acute dural venous sinus thrombosis and severe papilledema C.a 70-year old with bilateral, sequential non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy 10 years ago D.a 22-year old with bilateral vision loss from Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy 2 years ago. High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Optociliary shunt vessels (aka retinochoroidal collaterals) are a dilation of the naturally- occurring veins that drain from the peripapillary retinal circulation into the choroidal circulation. Which type of secreting pituitary adenoma is most likely to present with optic chiasm compression? A.Prolactin secreting adenoma B.Growth hormone (GH) secreting adenoma C.Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secreting adenoma D.Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) secreting adenoma High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Typically non-secreting adenomas present with vision loss much more commonly than secretory tumors because secretory tumors generally have systemic symptoms that allow them to be discovered before the tumor grows large enough for chiasmal compression to occur. GH secreting adenomas result in either gigantism or acromegaly depending on whether the patient has undergone puberty prior to development of the adenoma. ACTH secreting adenomas result in Cushing's syndrome and TSH secreting adenomas obviously result in hyperthyroidism. Prolactinomas, particularly in men, are much more likely to present later with chiasmal compression. Females with prolactinomas may present with galactorrhea, amenorrhea, or other menstrual cycle abnormalities. Prolactin secreting adenomas in men produce subtle symptoms of decreased libido and impotence. Because of these subtle symptoms (especially in men) the tumors are diagnosed at a later stage and tend to be larger at the time of diagnosis; it is not unusual for prolactin secreting adenomas to present with vision loss as a result. The other syndromes caused by secretory adenomas are quite noticeable and usually prompt an early work- up before the tumor grows to sufficient size to compress the optic chiasm. Thinning of which retinal layer can be used as a marker of disease burden in multiple sclerosis (MS)? A.Layer A B.Layer B C.Layer C D.Layer D High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: The anterior portion of the visual pathway consists of the axons that extend from the retinal ganglion cell nuclei (dark layer deep to layer B) to the nerve fiber layer to the optic nerves to the optic chiasm to the optic tract to the lateral geniculate nuclei where they synapse. MS is an idiopathic inflammatory CNS demyelinating disease that often affects the visual pathway fibers as they run in the optic nerve, optic chiasm, and optic tracts. OCT has enabled researchers to accurately measure the thickness of the nerve fiber layer (NFL). Research has conclusively shown that the NFL thickness is a reliable marker of health of the anterior visual pathway fibers. It likewise serves as a marker of disease burden in MS and can be used to follow progression of MS over time. Up to this point the utility of following NFL thickness in MS patients is mostly for research purposes. While the ganglion cell layer (GCL) was not an answer option, it is another retinal layer whose healthy is a correlate of MS disease burden. This makes sense, of course, considering that the NFL is made up of ganglion cell axons so if the axons are lost, the the cells that give rise to those axons have probably been lost also. Interestingly, even in patients with no history of optic neuritis or other afferent visual manifestations of MS, the OCT shows thinning of the NFL and GCL in MS patients suggesting that there is subclinical loss of ganglion cell axons in all patients with MS. Which of the following is not a symptom associated with intracranial pressure (ICP) elevation? A.transient visual obscurations lasting seconds with orthostatic changes B.chronic headaches C.scotomas with positive visual phenomena lasting 5-60 minutes D.pulsatile "whooshing" noise audible to the patient only High Yield: No Correct Answer: C Explanation: All of the above are characteristic of increased ICP except answer "C" Scotomas with positive visual phenomena lasting 5-60 minutes are characteristic of a visual aura that usually immediately precedes a migraine headache.

question: What is the the most appropriate step in acute management of this patient?
explanation: This patient is presenting with classic thyroid associated optic neuropathy. When associated with vision loss, thyroid associated orbitopathy requires immediate action. Medical management includes steroids to decrease extraocular muscle swelling. Surgical management includes orbital decompression surgery to remove one, two, or three walls of the orbit thereby expanding the orbital space. Often times steroids are a temporizing measure to prevent further optic nerve decline while surgical decompression is planned. A 60-year-old patient comes in with a complaint of intermittent binocular diplopia over the past 3 months. The video above documents what is observed when you ask the patient to look up for approximately 45 seconds. What is the most likely diagnosis based upon the exam shown in the video? Missing video A.Giant cell arteritis B.Myasthenia gravis C.Decompensated congenital exophoria D.Left microvascular cranial nerve 3 palsy High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: This video shows an absolutely classic example of levator palpebrae superioris (LPS) fatigue on prolonged upgaze testing- in this case occurring in the left eye. While such fatigue is not pathognomonic of myasthenia gravis, it is highly suggestive and should prompt further testing to conclusively confirm the diagnosis of myasthenia (anti-acetylcholine receptor (AchR) antibody testing, electromyography testing, or Tensilon testing). While not all findings of fatigue are as dramatic as in this case, the key to proper testing for fatigue is to perform the test for sufficient time to allow fatigue to occur. Some neuro-ophthalmologists say that prolonged upgaze testing is a competition between the examiner's arm and the patient to see who gets fatigued first. Prolonged upgaze testing should last at least one minute (which seems like an eternity in clinic) before calling a test negative. During upgaze testing the examiner should hold the patient’s head to ensure that he/she doesn’t lift the chin to avoid upgaze. Attention should be paid to both the eyelid position (assessing LPS fatigue) and globe position (assessing superior rectus fatigue) through the exam. Giant cell arteritis (GCA) can cause fatigue of the extraocular muscles or LPS due to ischemia of the extraocular muscles but typically this occurs in concert with or shortly prior to severe vision loss. While GCA can present with diplopia, it much more frequently occurs with vision loss from ischemic optic neuropathy or choroidal ischemia. Furthermore, GCA in a 60-year-old African American would be highly unlikely. While this patient who was later confirmed to have myasthenia gravis based on a positive AchR antibody did have an exotropia seen in the video, dramatic LPS fatigue is not an expected finding with a decompensated congenital exophoria. Likewise fatigue is not expected in a microvascular oculomotor nerve palsy. Furthermore, intermittent diplopia over 3 months is not the typical presentation for a microvascular oculomotor nerve palsy which generally presents acutely with sudden onset of diplopia that improves slowly over weeks to months. What is the pathophysiology behind most cases of optic neuropathy from thyroid-associated orbitopathy? A.Compression of the optic nerve at the orbital apex from enlarged extraocular muscles B.Proptosis with mechanical antero-posterior stretching of the nerve causing damage C.Mononuclear inflammatory cell infiltration of the optic nerve D.Optic nerve mitochondrial dysfunction from dysregulation of thyroid hormones High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: While there are many plausible explanations for optic neuropathy associated with thyroid associated orbitopathy, the generally accepted explanation is that extraocular muscles become engorged with inflammatory cells, fibrosis, and glycosaminoglycans. Near the bony orbital apex there is little room for expansion and the enlarged muscles compress the optic nerve as it enters the orbit. For this reason, it is not unusual to have cases of thyroid-associated optic neuropathy in patients with only mild proptosis. Some suggest that proptosis may actually be a protective process for the optic nerve by allowing the orbital volume to expand. Mononuclear cells do invade the extraocular muscles and lead to deposition of glycosaminoglycans, but the cause of optic neuropathy is not cellular invasion of the optic nerve. What is the only treatment proven with large randomized control trials to be successful for the prevention of sequential non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) in the contralateral eye of patients with monocular NAION? A.oral prednisone therapy B.Alphagan (brimonidine) drop therapy C.aspirin therapy D.there is no well-proven preventative therapy for NAION High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: There are two goals in treatment of NAION: 1) improve the visual recovery in the affected eye; and 2) prevent NAION in the contralateral eye. The Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial found optic nerve sheath decompression in eyes affected with NAION to increase the risk of moderate vision loss compared to observation. There is one controversial study suggesting prednisone therapy may improve visual recovery in NAION but this is not adopted by most neuro-ophthalmologists and does not purport to prevent NAION in the contralateral eye. Alphagan and aspirin have both been suggested as treatments to prevent sequential NAION but evidence supporting their use is scant. A 25-year-old female with no past medical history develops a painless unilateral scotoma in the temporal aspect of her right eye for the last 2 weeks. She vividly describes a flashing ring of lights along the margin of the scotoma. On exam, her central vision is 20/20 in both eyes and there is no afferent pupillary defect. Fundus exam is unremarkable and the optic nerves look healthy. Humprey visual field in the left eye is normal and in the right eye shows a 10-degree- wide cecocentral scotoma centered on the physiologic blind spot. What is the most appropriate next step in the care of this patient? A.multifocal ERG B.immediate admission for intravenous steroids C.reassurance with referral to a migraine specialist D.CT of the head and orbits High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This patient demonstrates a classic presentation of acute idiopathic blind-spot (IBS) syndrome. IBS syndrome typically is monocular, occurs more frequently in young women and presents with an enlarged blind spot scotoma and adjacent photopsias. Some have described IBS syndrome as a "waste basket" diagnosis because it probably includes numerous other diagnoses with subtle exam findings such as multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS) and acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR). In MEWDS, for instance, the presentation is nearly identical to IBS syndrome but there are characteristic small white dots on fundus exam. These small white dots only last days to weeks and can disappear before seen on examination. If the white dots are seen, the diagnosis made will likely be MEWDS. If a normal fundus is seen, the diagnosis made will likely be IBS syndrome. Similarly, AZOOR has a nearly identical presentation and is characterized by chorioretinal atrophy and pigment clumping around the optic nerve in the weeks to months after onset. In all of these syndromes, a multifocal ERG often shows focal areas of retinal dysfunction corresponding to the region of the patient's scotoma. While in theory this could be a presentation of optic neuritis prompting possible intravenous steroid treatment, the lack of pain and afferent pupillary defect make that diagnosis exceedingly unlikely. If one were to evaluate the patient for optic neuritis or other signs of demyelinating white matter disease, the scan of choice would be an MRI of the brain and orbits with and without IV contrast (not a CT of the brain and orbits). While this could simulate a scintillating scotoma of a migraine, migraine auras typically last 5 to 60 minutes and are usually associated with headache within an hour of the aura onset (though headache does not have to be present). 30-year-old Caucasian female presents with 1 week of malaise, fevers, bilateral facial palsy, and photophobia. Your examination shows bilateral non-granulomatous uveitis and the external exam findings displayed above. What is the name of the syndrome that this patient displays? A.Heerfordt syndrome B.Lofgren syndrome C.Raymond syndrome D.Claude syndrome High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: This patient displays the classic findings of Heerfordt syndrome (aka uveoparotid fever): uveitis, facial palsy (usually from parotid gland involvement / swelling as seen in this photo), and fever. Heerfordt syndrome is one of many ways that sarcoidosis can present. This particular presentation is not pathognomonic of sarcoidosis and the diagnosis must still be proven by excluding alternative etiologies and obtaining a biopsy sample that demonstrates granulomatous inflammation typical of sarcoid. Lofgren syndrome is another specific presentation of sarcoid characterized by the triad of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar adenopathy (usually diagnosed on chest imaging), and arthritis. Raymond syndrome and Claude syndrome are brainstem syndromes that are not specific for any one etiology but rather represent a constellation of findings attributable to a lesion affecting certain structures in the brainstem. Raymond syndrome is a 6th nerve palsy with a contralateral hemiparesis due to a lesion in the mid pons affecting the 6th nerve fasciculus along with the corticospinal tract. Claude syndrome is caused by damage to the dorsal midbrain affecting the superior cerebellar peduncle and 3rd nerve fasiculus typically resulting in ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy and contralateral ataxia. According to the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT), what percentage of patients with optic neuritis suffered from periocular pain in association with the optic neuritis attack? A.12% B.52% C.72% D.92% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: The optic neuritis treatment trial showed that 92% of optic neuritis cases have associated periocular pain. Due to this relatively-sensitive symptom, an absence of pain should raise doubt regarding the diagnosis of optic neuritis. A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden onset diplopia. He has a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus but reports no ocular history. Vision is 20/20 in both eyes and the anterior and posterior examination demonstrates no abnormalities. Motility examination demonstrates a complete left third nerve palsy. The patient undergoes immediate workup including MRI / MRA brain which demonstrates an acute infarction of the left cerebral peduncle. Which of the following additional examination findings would be expected? A.Right sided hemiparesis B.Right sided ataxia C.Left sided contralateral tremor and involuntary limb movements D.Convergence retraction saccades High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: An infarction of the cerebral peduncle with involvement of the third nerve fascicle is known as Weber syndrome. The nucleus of the third nerve is located in the dorsal midbrain and contains the subnuclei whose projecting fibers are destined for the bilateral levator palpebrae superioris muscles, ipsilateral medial rectus, ipsilateral inferior rectus, ipsilateral pupillary sphincter (via parasympathetics), and the contralateral superior rectus. A lesion involving the nucleus would therefore lead to a bilateral levator and superior rectus palsy and a complete ipsilateral third nerve palsy (see image). The projecting fibers (fascicle) then traverse ventrally passing near or through the red nucleus, substantia nigra, and cerebral peduncle to exit the midbrain. A lesion involving the fascicle and surrounding structures can produce a unilateral third palsy in addition to contralateral neurological signs based on the location; fascicular palsies may also be isolated. Historically, these lesions have been classified into several syndromes which have considerable variability in the literature, except for Weber syndrome which is consistently a lesion of the cerebral peduncle. Therefore, it is more useful to recognize the location of the lesion and resultant findings rather than the name of the syndrome. These lesions are classified as such: 1. Lesion of the cerebral peduncle: Contralateral hemiparesis due to involvement of the corticospinal tract within the cerebral peduncle (Weber syndrome) 2. Lesion of the red nucleus and substantia nigra: Contralateral ataxia or tremor / involuntary limb movements (Benedikt syndrome) 3. Lesion of decussating fibers from the superior cerebellar peduncle in the dorsal midbrain: Contralateral ataxia (Claude syndrome) 4. Dorsal midbrain lesion: CN III fascicular lesion + ipsilateral ataxia +/- some features of dorsal midbrain syndrome (e.g., vertical gaze paresis, convergence retraction saccades, skew deviation, and lid retraction) (Nothnagel syndrome) The typical cause of these syndromes is infarction in the territory of a paramedian penetrating vessel arising from the proximal posterior cerebral artery. WRONG ANSWERS: • (Choice B): A contralateral ataxia would be possible in one of the other three syndromes, but involvement of only the cerebral peduncle should not produce a contralateral ataxia. • (Choice C): Common to all of these syndromes is an ipsilateral third nerve palsy in addition to contralateral neurologic signs. • (Choice D): Convergence retraction saccades can be found in a dorsal midbrain syndrome but would not be expected in a lesion of the cerebral peduncle. REFERENCE: Liu GT, Crenner CW, Logigian EL, Charness ME, Samuels MA. Midbrain syndromes of Benedikt, Claude, and Nothnagel: setting the record straight. Neurology. 1992 Sep;42(9):1820-2.

A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden onset diplopia. He has a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus but reports no ocular history. Vision is 20/20 in both eyes and the anterior and posterior examination demonstrates no abnormalities. Motility examination demonstrates a complete left third nerve palsy. The patient undergoes immediate workup including MRI / MRA brain which demonstrates an acute infarction of the left cerebral peduncle. The nucleus of the third nerve is located in the dorsal midbrain and contains the subnuclei whose projecting fibers are destined for the bilateral levator palpebrae superioris muscles, ipsilateral medial rectus, ipsilateral inferior rectus, ipsilateral pupillary sphincter (via parasympathetics), and the contralateral superior rectus. A lesion involving the nucleus would therefore lead to a bilateral levator and superior rectus palsy and a complete ipsilateral third nerve palsy (see image). The projecting fibers (fascicle) then traverse ventrally passing near or through the red nucleus, substantia nigra, and cerebral peduncle to exit the midbrain. A lesion involving the fascicle and surrounding structures can produce a unilateral third palsy in addition to contralateral neurological signs based on the location; fascicular palsies may also be isolated. Historically, these lesions have been classified into several syndromes which have considerable variability in the literature, except for Weber syndrome which is consistently a lesion of the cerebral peduncle. Therefore, it is more useful to recognize the location of the lesion and resultant findings rather than the name of the syndrome. These lesions are classified as such: 1. Lesion of the cerebral peduncle: Contralateral hemiparesis due to involvement of the corticospinal tract within the cerebral peduncle (Weber syndrome) 2. Lesion of the red nucleus and substantia nigra: Contralateral ataxia or tremor / involuntary limb movements (Benedikt syndrome) 3. Lesion of decussating fibers from the superior cerebellar peduncle in the dorsal midbrain: Contralateral ataxia (Claude syndrome) 4. WRONG ANSWERS: • (Choice B): A contralateral ataxia would be possible in one of the other three syndromes, but involvement of only the cerebral peduncle should not produce a contralateral ataxia. • (Choice C): Common to all of these syndromes is an ipsilateral third nerve palsy in addition to contralateral neurologic signs. • (Choice D): Convergence retraction saccades can be found in a dorsal midbrain syndrome but would not be expected in a lesion of the cerebral peduncle. question: What is the pathophysiology behind most cases of optic neuropathy from thyroid-associated orbitopathy?

options.A: Compression of the optic nerve at the orbital apex from enlarged extraocular muscles
options.B: Proptosis with mechanical antero-posterior stretching of the nerve causing damage
options.C: Mononuclear inflammatory cell infiltration of the optic nerve
options.D: Optic nerve mitochondrial dysfunction from dysregulation of thyroid hormones

explanation: While there are many plausible explanations for optic neuropathy associated with thyroid associated orbitopathy, the generally accepted explanation is that extraocular muscles become engorged with inflammatory cells, fibrosis, and glycosaminoglycans. Near the bony orbital apex there is little room for expansion and the enlarged muscles compress the optic nerve as it enters the orbit. For this reason, it is not unusual to have cases of thyroid-associated optic neuropathy in patients with only mild proptosis. Some suggest that proptosis may actually be a protective process for the optic nerve by allowing the orbital volume to expand. Mononuclear cells do invade the extraocular muscles and lead to deposition of glycosaminoglycans, but the cause of optic neuropathy is not cellular invasion of the optic nerve. What is the only treatment proven with large randomized control trials to be successful for the prevention of sequential non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) in the contralateral eye of patients with monocular NAION? A.oral prednisone therapy B.Alphagan (brimonidine) drop therapy C.aspirin therapy D.there is no well-proven preventative therapy for NAION High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: There are two goals in treatment of NAION: 1) improve the visual recovery in the affected eye; and 2) prevent NAION in the contralateral eye. The Ischemic Optic Neuropathy Decompression Trial found optic nerve sheath decompression in eyes affected with NAION to increase the risk of moderate vision loss compared to observation. There is one controversial study suggesting prednisone therapy may improve visual recovery in NAION but this is not adopted by most neuro-ophthalmologists and does not purport to prevent NAION in the contralateral eye. Alphagan and aspirin have both been suggested as treatments to prevent sequential NAION but evidence supporting their use is scant.
